query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting approximately 25 at.% Al into a near-equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy and then applying a high-temperature solution treatment followed by controlled aging will induce partial B2 ordering within the FCC matrix, generating nanoprecipitates that act as domain wall pinning centers and thereby increase the coercivity relative to FeCoNi and its Pd/Pt derivatives.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase FCC FeCoNi high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~25 at.% Al to form a FeCoNiAl alloy.
generation.conditions: Synthesize the alloy by conventional methods (e.g., arc-melting), then solution-treat at 1100–1200°C and age at 500–600°C, ensuring that the high configurational entropy (≥1.0R) is maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed B2-ordered nanoprecipitates or partially ordered regions embedded within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The partial B2 ordering creates internal interfaces that serve as pinning sites for magnetic domain walls. This enhanced pinning increases coercivity while preserving high saturation magnetization, in contrast to the soft magnetic behavior of pure FeCoNi and its Pd/Pt derivatives.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the specified thermal processing conditions, the FeCoNiAl alloy is expected to display a measurable increase in coercivity compared to the FeCoNi baseline and reported FeCoNiPd/FeCoNiPt alloys, with the high saturation magnetization largely retained.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic FeCoNi high-entropy alloy and its Pd/Pt derivatives, which exhibit soft ferromagnetism with low coercive fields.
generation.boundary: The effect is anticipated only within near-equiatomic compositions that preserve high configurational entropy; conditions leading to complete phase transformation or excessive grain growth (which might either eliminate controlled B2 ordering or degrade the magnetic properties) fall outside the expected regime.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the coercivity increase and the balance with saturation magnetization depend on the extent, size, and distribution of the B2-ordered regions—all of which require optimization in further experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one control sample of equiatomic FeCoNi and one FeCoNiAl alloy with ~25 at.% Al. Subject both to identical processing procedures, including solution treatment at 1100–1200°C and aging at 500–600°C. Characterize the microstructure via X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy to confirm the presence of partial B2 ordering in the Al-doped sample. Measure the magnetic hysteresis loops at room temperature to evaluate coercivity and saturation magnetization.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns (to detect B2 ordering)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeCoNiAl samples do not show a statistically significant increase (e.g., >20% increase) in coercivity relative to the control FeCoNi samples, or if the Al addition results in an unacceptable drop in saturation magnetization, then the hypothesis that partial B2 ordering enhances coercivity via domain wall pinning is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloy nanopowders were successfully prepared by liquid-phase reduction methods and their applications were preliminarily discussed. The prepared high entropy alloy nanopowders consisted of FeNi alloy spherical powders and NiFeCoCrY alloy spherical powders with a particle size of about 100 nm. The powders have soft magnetic properties, the saturation magnetization field strength were up to 5000 Qe and the saturation magnetization strength Ms was about 17.3 emu/g. The powders have the excellent property of low high-frequency loss in the frequency range of 0.3–8.5 GHz. When the thickness of the powders coating was 5 mm, the powders showed excellent absorption performance in the Ku band; and when the thickness of the powders coating was 10 mm; the powders showed good wave-absorbing performance in the X band. The powders have good moulding, and the powders have large specific surface area, so that the magnetic powder core composites could be prepared under low pressure and without coating insulators, and the magnetic powder cores showed excellent frequency-constant magnetization and magnetic field-constant magnetization characteristics. While the combination of saturation magnetization and coercivity for these RTA‐ treated FeCoNiMnCu films is impressive in comparison to previously reported bulk systems, the coercivity is still modest, due to the high symmetry of the cubic lattice which limits the intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy. The facilitation of low‐symmetry chemical order and crystal structure combined with strong spin‐orbit coupling is in general necessary to realize strong magnetocrysalline anisotropy. To achieve these conditions in a high entropy system, we have added 50 at.% Pt to the FeCoNiMnCu alloy, employing the high entropy intermetallic design approach in search of highly anisotropic L10 ordering. Although the certainty of Pt sites reduces the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, we demonstrate below that such optimized entropy can still stabilize a single high‐entropy L10 phase.

The saturation magnetization (MS) and coercivity (Hc) for the four different samples analyzed in the present study have been listed in Table 1. The MS of AlCoFeNi is substantially higher compared to that of the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy for both heat-treated conditions. While the magnetization is primarily determined by composition and the crystal structure, the coercivity can be affected by impurities, deformation, grain size and phase decomposition. The coercivity (Hc) decreased with increasing annealing temperature from 15 Oe for sample aged at 600 °C/15 h, exhibiting nanoscale phase separation, to 4 Oe for samples aged at 1000 °C/15 h, exhibiting a homogeneous undecomposed B2 matrix. A similar observation has been reported in the literature, where the coercivity of the AlCoCrCuFeNi HEA annealed at 1000 °C/2 h decreases by 30 Oe (from 45 Oe to 15 Oe) compared to as-cast alloys. decision.trend: Over several attempts to enhance the magnetic performance of FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys, researchers introduced Al (often with additional elements like Si, Cu, Sn, or Ta) to form B2 or BCC-type phases and precipitates within a primarily FCC matrix. These modifications partially improved coercivity through localized domain-wall pinning without drastically degrading saturation magnetization. Early efforts focused on soft magnetic properties, and even when Al was introduced, the systems often included multiple alloying elements or required tailored magnetic-field processing strategies, leaving open the question of how to selectively boost coercivity by controlled partial ordering. While coherent B2 nanoprecipitates are known to enhance mechanical properties with minimal losses in soft magnetism, a direct demonstration of using partial B2 ordering to achieve a significant coercivity increase in a strictly near-equiatomic FeCoNi alloy has yet to be conclusively shown.
decision.unsolved: A persistent gap is the lack of a straightforward, single-step doping approach that leverages partial B2 ordering in an otherwise high-entropy FeCoNi matrix to substantially increase domain-wall pinning (and thus coercivity) while preserving high saturation magnetization and meeting the 1.0R configurational entropy criterion.
decision.lever: Introduce Al in a near-equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy (e.g., Fe25Co25Ni25Al25), followed by solution treating at ~1100–1200 °C and aging at ~500–600 °C to induce a fine dispersion of B2-ordered precipitates or partially ordered regions.
decision.why: Building on earlier demonstrations that Al additions in FeCoNi-based HEAs can form B2-type ordering, the proposed approach is to exploit partially ordered regions that pin domain walls, thereby increasing coercivity. This should preserve high configurational entropy (≥1.0R) and the overall near-equiatomic composition while enhancing ordering-driven anisotropy without excessive loss of saturation magnetization. A discriminating experiment would compare coercivity and saturation magnetization of Al-containing aged samples versus an Al-free FeCoNi reference under controlled conditions (same heat treatments, same grain size). If no measurable increase in coercivity or if there is a disproportionately large drop in saturation magnetization, then this mechanism would be falsified.
